context: core & riser-led · vertical transport & life-safety commissioning

brief.intro: A commercial high-rise or mixed-use tower is defined by its vertical concrete or steel core, which climbs floor by floor ahead of the surrounding structure, and by the MEP risers and lifts that run through it to serve every level above. Unlike a low-rise building, the programme is governed by the speed of the core-and-floor cycle — how many floors per week the structure can climb — because every trade behind it (risers, envelope, fit-out) is paced by that front. Vertical transportation (lifts and escalators) must be installed in step with the core, since it is needed both for construction hoisting and for the building's final life-safety system. That life-safety system — fire detection, sprinklers, smoke control and stair pressurisation working together as one integrated cause-and-effect test — is usually what decides the handover date, not the structure itself.

scope.desc: Shoring, basement excavation, piling/raft foundations and waterproofing.

scope.name: Core & superstructure
scope.desc: Jump-form or slip-form core climb with a repeating floor-by-floor structural cycle (columns, slabs, decking).

scope.name: Building envelope / facade
scope.desc: Curtain wall or cladding system following the structural cycle up the building.

scope.name: Vertical MEP risers
scope.desc: Power, water, drainage and HVAC ductwork/pipework distributed through dedicated shafts, floor to floor.

scope.name: Mechanical — HVAC & chilled water
scope.desc: Central plant (chillers, cooling towers) plus floor-by-floor AHU/FCU distribution.

scope.name: Electrical power & lighting
scope.desc: Incoming substation, LV distribution, standby generator, floor panels and lighting.

scope.name: Fire protection & life safety
scope.desc: Sprinklers, standpipes, fire alarm, smoke control and stair pressurisation.

scope.name: Vertical transportation
scope.desc: Lift and escalator installation, following the core with a floor-by-floor shaft handover.

scope.name: ELV / BMS
scope.desc: Structured cabling, security, and the building management system tying HVAC, power and fire together.

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & occupancy handover
scope.desc: Floor-by-floor system proving, the integrated fire/life-safety matrix test, and the base-build to fit-out interface.

glossary.plain: the central concrete or steel structure (lift shafts, stairs, risers) that climbs ahead of the floor slabs and anchors the whole building.
fast-climbing formwork systems used to build the core continuously, floor by floor.
a vertical shaft carrying power, water, drainage or air from the plant rooms to every floor.
fans that push air into stairwells during a fire so smoke cannot enter the escape route.
the rulebook proving that each fire event (e.g. a smoke detector on floor 12) triggers exactly the right response — alarms, dampers, lift recall, smoke fans — building-wide.
the landlord's core-and-shell work versus the tenant's own interior fit-out, usually built by different teams on different schedules.
the regulatory sign-off, usually gated by the integrated fire/life-safety test, that allows people to occupy the building.

must_get_right: The core-and-floor cycle sets the pace for everything behind it — track floors-per-week, not just overall percent complete.
Vertical risers must be coordinated and installed as the core climbs; a missed riser sleeve or shaft opening is far more expensive to fix later than to plan for.
The integrated fire/life-safety cause-and-effect test is the real gate to occupancy — protect time and contingency for it, and expect re-tests.
Keep the base-build and tenant fit-out schedules clearly separated but coordinated at the interface (risers, floor loading, shaft access).

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The floor-by-floor structural and MEP cycles are typically modelled with a repeating 'typical floor' duration rather than fully discrete activities per level. The network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones; total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Core climb often runs a continuous or 6-day cycle to hold its pace; typical-floor MEP and envelope trades run 6-day, moving to two shifts where needed to keep pace with the core; commissioning runs against inspection and authority availability. A weather allowance is embedded for facade and high-level work.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The core climb sets the pace: the critical path typically runs core-and-floor cycle → riser installation following a fixed number of floors behind → floor MEP fit-out → integrated fire/life-safety test → occupancy certificate. Vertical transportation (lifts) installation must keep pace with the core since it is needed both for construction hoisting and for the final life-safety interface.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Facade design is frozen per typical floor; a single, sustained core-climb rate is maintained; tenant fit-out is excluded from the base-build baseline and interfaces at defined handover points; one lift contractor is mobilised early enough to follow the core.

rows: Before envelope follow-up on each floor

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Tower-crane capacity and hoisting sequence govern material delivery to height; congested city-centre sites often have limited laydown; riser-shaft access must be coordinated across multiple trades working simultaneously; vertical hoist capacity is shared and a common late-stage constraint.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: core-climb rate slippage, which cascades to every floor behind it; re-test loops on the fire cause-and-effect matrix; facade lead-time slippage. Schedule contingency is held before the integrated fire/life-safety test and before the occupancy inspection, rather than spread thinly across floors.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
